warmup.q: A Netty server runs 2 worker event loops. Six clients connect. The handler for client 3 calls a JDBC query that takes 500 ms. Which clients notice?
options: The clients that share client 3's event loop, roughly half of them
All six clients, because Netty serializes the whole server
None of them: Netty runs each read on a fresh thread
warmup.why: Netty assigns each new channel to one loop of the group, round-robin, and keeps it there for life. Every handler call for those channels runs on that loop's one thread. Clients 1, 3 and 5 share a loop, so 1 and 5 wait behind client 3's query. The clients on the other loop never notice.

sections.h: An event loop is one thread that owns its channels
sections.html:
Netty is the select loop from the last lesson, written once and written well. Each piece you wrote by hand has a Netty name, and each fixes a bug you met there:

Your loop in lesson 2 Netty Why it exists
one thread running select() EventLoop, several in an EventLoopGroup one loop per core instead of one per server
the Conn attachment Channel and its ChannelPipeline of handlers per-connection state and logic in small pieces
flip() and compact() by hand ByteBuf, with separate read and write indexes no mode to get wrong (lesson 4)
pending bytes and arming OP_WRITE the channel's outbound buffer Netty sets and clears OP_WRITE for you
dropping OP_READ when full autoRead and writability backpressure as a setting (lesson 4)
nothing: only the loop may touch the selector a task queue on every loop any thread can hand the loop work safely

So an event loop is one thread that runs a selector over many channels, plus that queue of tasks. In Netty 4.2 you build a group by naming the IO handler, the transport-specific part:

Java
EventLoopGroup boss = new MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup(1, NioIoHandler.newFactory());   // accepts connections
EventLoopGroup workers = new MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup(NioIoHandler.newFactory());  // serves them
Channel server = new ServerBootstrap()
        .group(boss, workers)
        .channel(NioServerSocketChannel.class)
        .childHandler(new ChannelInitializer<SocketChannel>() {
            @Override
            protected void initChannel(SocketChannel ch) {
                ch.pipeline().addLast(new LineBasedFrameDecoder(64), new StringDecoder(UTF_8),
                        new StringEncoder(UTF_8), new QuoteHandler());
            }
        })
        .bind(8080).sync().channel();
Kotlin
val boss = MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup(1, NioIoHandler.newFactory())     // accepts connections
val workers = MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup(NioIoHandler.newFactory())    // serves them
val server = ServerBootstrap()
    .group(boss, workers)
    .channel(NioServerSocketChannel::class.java)
    .childHandler(object : ChannelInitializer<SocketChannel>() {
        override fun initChannel(ch: SocketChannel) {
            ch.pipeline().addLast(LineBasedFrameDecoder(64), StringDecoder(UTF_8),
                StringEncoder(UTF_8), QuoteHandler())
        }
    })
    .bind(8080).sync().channel()

If you learned Netty 4.1, you wrote new NioEventLoopGroup(). Netty 4.2 deprecated it, along with its epoll and kqueue cousins, and javac -Xlint:deprecation says so: warning: [deprecation] NioEventLoopGroup in io.netty.channel.nio has been deprecated. The replacement is always MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup plus a factory: NioIoHandler, EpollIoHandler, KQueueIoHandler or IoUringIoHandler. The bootstrap still names the matching channel class.

The boss group only accepts connections and hands each one to a worker loop, so one boss thread is plenty for one listening port. Small servers often pass a single group to .group(group) and let the same loops accept and serve. The lab does that, with one loop, so that you can see a blocked loop clearly.

Without a thread count, a group gets two loops per core, so the demo prints 8 on a 4-core machine. Each new connection is registered with one loop, round-robin, and stays there for life:

client port 59604 registered on multiThreadIoEventLoopGroup-4-1, inEventLoop=true
client port 59620 registered on multiThreadIoEventLoopGroup-4-2, inEventLoop=true
client port 59634 registered on multiThreadIoEventLoopGroup-4-1, inEventLoop=true

That pinning is why Netty handlers rarely need locks: every event for a channel runs on its loop's one thread, one after another. It is also why one slow handler hurts. Every other channel on that loop waits behind it.

try.title: See which loop owns each connection
steps: Open EventLoopDemo.java (or EventLoopDemo.kt). It starts a server with one acceptor loop and two worker loops, then connects four clients one after another.
Predict the thread name for the third and fourth client, and what inEventLoop() returns inside the handler.
Run it. Then change the worker group to new MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup(1, ...) and run it again.

code.html: package workbench.nio.l03; import io.netty.bootstrap.ServerBootstrap; import io.netty.channel.Channel; import io.netty.channel.ChannelHandlerContext; import io.netty.channel.ChannelInboundHandlerAdapter; import io.netty.channel.ChannelInitializer; import io.netty.channel.EventLoopGroup; import io.netty.channel.MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup; import io.netty.channel.nio.NioIoHandler; import io.netty.channel.socket.SocketChannel; import io.netty.channel.socket.nio.NioServerSocketChannel; import java.io.InputStream; import java.net.InetAddress; import java.net.InetSocketAddress; import java.net.Socket; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** Which event-loop thread serves each connection? One acceptor loop, two worker loops, four clients. */ public class EventLoopDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup defaults = new MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup(NioIoHandler.newFactory()); System.out.println("default loop count: " + defaults.executorCount() + " (availableProcessors=" + Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors() + ")"); defaults.shutdownGracefully(0, 0, TimeUnit.SECONDS).sync(); EventLoopGroup boss = new MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup(1, NioIoHandler.newFactory()); // accepts EventLoopGroup workers = new MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup(2, NioIoHandler.newFactory()); // serves try { Channel server = new ServerBootstrap() .group(boss, workers) .channel(NioServerSocketChannel.class) .childHandler(new ChannelInitializer<SocketChannel>() { @Override protected void initChannel(SocketChannel ch) { ch.pipeline().addLast(new ChannelInboundHandlerAdapter() { @Override public void channelActive(ChannelHandlerContext ctx) { System.out.printf("client port %d registered on %s, inEventLoop=%s%n", ((InetSocketAddress) ctx.channel().remoteAddress()).getPort(), Thread.currentThread().getName(), ctx.channel().eventLoop().inEventLoop()); } @Override public void channelRead(ChannelHandlerContext ctx, Object msg) { System.out.printf(" bytes from port %d handled on %s%n", ((InetSocketAddress) ctx.channel().remoteAddress()).getPort(), Thread.currentThread().getName()); ctx.writeAndFlush(msg); // echo: the write takes ownership of msg, no release here } }); } }) .bind(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), 0).sync().channel(); int port = ((InetSocketAddress) server.localAddress()).getPort(); for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) { try (Socket client = new Socket(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), port)) { client.getOutputStream().write("hi".getBytes()); InputStream in = client.getInputStream(); in.readNBytes(2); } } server.close().sync(); } finally { boss.shutdownGracefully(0, 1, TimeUnit.SECONDS).sync(); workers.shutdownGracefully(0, 1, TimeUnit.SECONDS).sync(); } } }

sections.h: The pipeline: reads flow in, writes flow out
sections.html:
Every channel has a ChannelPipeline: a linked list of handlers between a head, next to the socket, and a tail. Two kinds of traffic move through it.

Each handler gets a ChannelHandlerContext, usually called ctx: its own slot in the pipeline, with methods to pass an event to the next handler or to start a write from that slot. Inbound events start at the head and move toward the tail: channelActive when the connection opens, channelRead for each message, channelReadComplete after a batch of reads, and exceptionCaught when something fails. Inbound handlers transform the message on its way. In the quote server, the frame decoder turns a stream of bytes into one ByteBuf per line, and StringDecoder turns that into a String, so the last handler only ever sees whole lines.

Outbound operations go the other way. write, flush and close start where you call them and move toward the head. StringEncoder sits on that path and turns your String back into bytes. So the order of addLast is the order inbound events see the handlers, and the reverse of the order writes see them.

One detail decides which handlers a write passes. ctx.writeAndFlush(msg) starts at the current handler and goes toward the head, skipping everything after it. ctx.channel().writeAndFlush(msg) starts at the tail and passes every outbound handler. Inside a handler, use ctx unless you really want the whole pipeline.

This section's demo puts a tap between the stages and feeds one line in pieces:

writeInbound("hel")
writeInbound("lo\nwor")
   in,  after framing : ByteBuf "hello"
   in,  business sees : String "hello"
   out, to the wire   : ByteBuf "HELLO\n"
100-byte line -> TooLongFrameException: frame length (100) exceeds the allowed maximum (64)
finish() = false

The first fragment produced nothing: the decoder kept the bytes and waited for the end of the line. That is lesson 2's framing problem, solved once inside the pipeline. The 64-byte limit matters as much. Without it, a client that never sends a newline makes the decoder buffer forever.

The demo uses EmbeddedChannel, which runs a pipeline with no socket and no real event loop. writeInbound pushes bytes in, readOutbound returns what the handlers wrote, and finish() says whether anything was left over. It is the fastest way to test a handler, and this lesson's lab uses it.

figure.caption: Reads travel from the head through the decoders to your handler; your writes travel back through the encoder to the head. One thread runs all of it.

try.title: Move the tap past the encoder
steps: Run PipelineDemo (or PipelineDemoKt) and match each printed line to a handler in the figure.
In the EmbeddedChannel constructor, move the outbound tap so it comes right after new StringEncoder(UTF_8) instead of before it.
Predict what out, to the wire prints now, then run it again.

code.html: package workbench.nio.l03; import io.netty.buffer.ByteBuf; import io.netty.buffer.Unpooled; import io.netty.channel.ChannelHandlerContext; import io.netty.channel.ChannelInboundHandlerAdapter; import io.netty.channel.ChannelOutboundHandlerAdapter; import io.netty.channel.ChannelPromise; import io.netty.channel.SimpleChannelInboundHandler; import io.netty.channel.embedded.EmbeddedChannel; import io.netty.handler.codec.LineBasedFrameDecoder; import io.netty.handler.codec.string.StringDecoder; import io.netty.handler.codec.string.StringEncoder; import java.util.List; import static java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets.UTF_8; /** Feeds bytes into a pipeline in fragments and prints what each stage sees, inbound and outbound. */ public class PipelineDemo { static String describe(Object msg) { String text = msg instanceof ByteBuf b ? b.toString(UTF_8) : msg.toString(); String type = msg instanceof ByteBuf ? "ByteBuf" : msg.getClass().getSimpleName(); return type + " \"" + text.replace("\n", "\\n") + "\""; } public static void main(String[] args) { EmbeddedChannel ch = new EmbeddedChannel( new LineBasedFrameDecoder(64), // inbound: bytes -> one ByteBuf per line new ChannelInboundHandlerAdapter() { // inbound tap @Override public void channelRead(ChannelHandlerContext ctx, Object msg) { System.out.println(" in, after framing : " + describe(msg)); ctx.fireChannelRead(msg); // pass it on (ownership moves with it) } }, new StringDecoder(UTF_8), // inbound: ByteBuf -> String new ChannelOutboundHandlerAdapter() { // outbound tap, nearer the head than the encoder @Override public void write(ChannelHandlerContext ctx, Object msg, ChannelPromise promise) { System.out.println(" out, to the wire : " + describe(msg)); ctx.write(msg, promise); } }, new StringEncoder(UTF_8), // outbound: String -> ByteBuf new SimpleChannelInboundHandler<String>() { // business logic, last @Override protected void channelRead0(ChannelHandlerContext ctx, String line) { System.out.println(" in, business sees : String \"" + line + "\""); ctx.writeAndFlush(line.toUpperCase() + "\n"); // travels toward the head } }); for (String fragment : List.of("hel", "lo\nwor", "ld\n")) { System.out.println("writeInbound(\"" + fragment.replace("\n", "\\n") + "\")"); ch.writeInbound(Unpooled.copiedBuffer(fragment, UTF_8)); ByteBuf out; while ((out = ch.readOutbound()) != null) out.release(); } try { ch.writeInbound(Unpooled.copiedBuffer("x".repeat(100) + "\n", UTF_8)); } catch (Exception e) { System.out.println("100-byte line -> " + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + ": " + e.getMessage()); } System.out.println("finish() = " + ch.finish()); } }

try.expect: Before the move the tap prints ByteBuf "HELLO\n": the write passed the encoder first. After the move it prints String "HELLO\n", because the write now reaches the tap before the encoder. Writes travel from the business handler toward the head, so position in the list decides what each outbound handler sees.

sections.html:
Handlers run on the event-loop thread. A handler that sleeps, waits on a lock, or calls JDBC holds that thread, and every other channel on the loop waits with it. This section's demo measures it with one event loop and two clients. Client A asks for SLOW, which sleeps 1 s to stand in for a database call. Client B asks for FAST 50 ms later:

[blocking in the handler]
   event-loop lag probe: 1010 ms
   FAST reply after 1011 ms: FAST on multiThreadIoEventLoopGroup-2-1
[dispatch to app pool]
   event-loop lag probe: 0 ms
   FAST reply after 2 ms: FAST on app-blocking-pool

The lag probe is a trick worth keeping: submit an empty task to the loop and time how long it waits to run. On a healthy loop it is close to 0.

Netty 4.1 offered a shortcut: pipeline.addLast(executorGroup, "name", handler) ran one handler on a separate EventExecutorGroup. Netty 4.2 deprecated those overloads, and compiling the old call prints warning: [deprecation] addLast(EventExecutorGroup,String,ChannelHandler) in ChannelPipeline has been deprecated. The commit that did it (d64340b) says per-handler executors caused more problems than they solved and that it is "much better to dispatch it manually".

Manual dispatch is three lines. Hand the slow part to your own executor and write the reply from there:

Java
@Override
protected void channelRead0(ChannelHandlerContext ctx, String line) {
    blockingPool.execute(() -> {                   // 1. leave the event loop
        String quote = quoteDao.findQuote(line);   // 2. block here: JDBC, a 120 ms issuer call
        ctx.writeAndFlush(quote + "\n");           // 3. safe from any thread
    });
}
Kotlin
override fun channelRead0(ctx: ChannelHandlerContext, line: String) {
    blockingPool.execute {                         // 1. leave the event loop
        val quote = quoteDao.findQuote(line)       // 2. block here: JDBC, a 120 ms issuer call
        ctx.writeAndFlush("$quote\n")              // 3. safe from any thread
    }
}

Step 3 works because Netty checks inEventLoop() on every write. Called from another thread, the write becomes a task on the channel's own loop, so the pipeline still runs on one thread. If code in the executor needs the handler's own fields, hop back first with ctx.executor().execute(...), so that state stays confined to the loop. Size blockingPool like any blocking pool: Little's law and the downstream's limits from lesson 1, or virtual threads.

try.title: Block the loop, then free it
steps: Open BlockingLoopDemo.java (or BlockingLoopDemo.kt). Predict the lag probe and the FAST reply time in both runs.
Run it with the command below.
In the blocking run, which thread produced the SLOW reply? In the dispatch run? Find the line in the code that decides it.

code.title: BlockingLoopDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.nio.l03; import io.netty.bootstrap.ServerBootstrap; import io.netty.channel.Channel; import io.netty.channel.ChannelHandlerContext; import io.netty.channel.ChannelInitializer; import io.netty.channel.EventLoopGroup; import io.netty.channel.MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup; import io.netty.channel.SimpleChannelInboundHandler; import io.netty.channel.nio.NioIoHandler; import io.netty.channel.socket.SocketChannel; import io.netty.channel.socket.nio.NioServerSocketChannel; import io.netty.handler.codec.LineBasedFrameDecoder; import io.netty.handler.codec.string.StringDecoder; import io.netty.handler.codec.string.StringEncoder; import java.io.BufferedReader; import java.io.InputStreamReader; import java.net.InetAddress; import java.net.InetSocketAddress; import java.net.Socket; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import static java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets.UTF_8; /** One event loop. Client A asks for SLOW (a 1 s "JDBC call"); client B asks for FAST 50 ms later. */ public class BlockingLoopDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { run(false); run(true); } static String work(String line) throws InterruptedException { if (line.equals("SLOW")) Thread.sleep(1_000); // stands in for a blocking JDBC call return line + " on " + Thread.currentThread().getName(); } static void run(boolean dispatch) throws Exception { EventLoopGroup group = new MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup(1, NioIoHandler.newFactory()); ExecutorService blockingPool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4, r -> new Thread(r, "app-blocking-pool")); try { Channel server = new ServerBootstrap().group(group).channel(NioServerSocketChannel.class) .childHandler(new ChannelInitializer<SocketChannel>() { @Override protected void initChannel(SocketChannel ch) { ch.pipeline().addLast(new LineBasedFrameDecoder(1024), new StringDecoder(UTF_8), new StringEncoder(UTF_8), new SimpleChannelInboundHandler<String>() { @Override protected void channelRead0(ChannelHandlerContext ctx, String line) throws Exception { if (!dispatch) { ctx.writeAndFlush(work(line) + "\n"); // blocks the event loop return; } blockingPool.execute(() -> { // leave the loop for the slow part String reply; try { reply = work(line); } catch (InterruptedException e) { reply = "interrupted"; } ctx.writeAndFlush(reply + "\n"); // safe from any thread }); } }); } }) .bind(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), 0).sync().channel(); int port = ((InetSocketAddress) server.localAddress()).getPort(); try (Socket a = new Socket(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), port); Socket b = new Socket(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), port)) { BufferedReader aIn = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(a.getInputStream(), UTF_8)); BufferedReader bIn = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(b.getInputStream(), UTF_8)); a.getOutputStream().write("SLOW\n".getBytes(UTF_8)); Thread.sleep(50); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); b.getOutputStream().write("FAST\n".getBytes(UTF_8)); // lag probe: how long until a trivial task runs on the loop? long lagMs = group.next().submit(() -> (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000).get(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS); String fast = bIn.readLine(); long fastMs = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; System.out.println(dispatch ? "[dispatch to app pool]" : "[blocking in the handler]"); System.out.printf(" event-loop lag probe: %d ms%n", lagMs); System.out.printf(" FAST reply after %d ms: %s%n", fastMs, fast); System.out.printf(" SLOW reply: %s%n", aIn.readLine()); } server.close().sync(); } finally { group.shutdownGracefully(0, 1, TimeUnit.SECONDS).sync(); // close channels and loops first... blockingPool.shutdown(); // ...then the pool they write from } } }

alt.title: BlockingLoopDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.nio.l03 import io.netty.bootstrap.ServerBootstrap import io.netty.channel.ChannelHandlerContext import io.netty.channel.ChannelInitializer import io.netty.channel.MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup import io.netty.channel.SimpleChannelInboundHandler import io.netty.channel.nio.NioIoHandler import io.netty.channel.socket.SocketChannel import io.netty.channel.socket.nio.NioServerSocketChannel import io.netty.handler.codec.LineBasedFrameDecoder import io.netty.handler.codec.string.StringDecoder import io.netty.handler.codec.string.StringEncoder import java.net.InetAddress import java.net.InetSocketAddress import java.net.Socket import java.util.concurrent.Callable import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit import kotlin.text.Charsets.UTF_8 /** One event loop. Client A asks for SLOW (a 1 s "JDBC call"); client B asks for FAST 50 ms later. */ fun main() { runLoop(dispatch = false) runLoop(dispatch = true) } private fun slowWork(line: String): String { if (line == "SLOW") Thread.sleep(1_000) // stands in for a blocking JDBC call return "$line on ${Thread.currentThread().name}" } private fun runLoop(dispatch: Boolean) { val group = MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup(1, NioIoHandler.newFactory()) val blockingPool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4) { r -> Thread(r, "app-blocking-pool") } try { val server = ServerBootstrap().group(group).channel(NioServerSocketChannel::class.java) .childHandler(object : ChannelInitializer<SocketChannel>() { override fun initChannel(ch: SocketChannel) { ch.pipeline().addLast(LineBasedFrameDecoder(1024), StringDecoder(UTF_8), StringEncoder(UTF_8), object : SimpleChannelInboundHandler<String>() { override fun channelRead0(ctx: ChannelHandlerContext, line: String) { if (!dispatch) { ctx.writeAndFlush(slowWork(line) + "\n") // blocks the event loop return } blockingPool.execute { // leave the loop for the slow part ctx.writeAndFlush(slowWork(line) + "\n") // safe from any thread } } }) } }) .bind(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), 0).sync().channel() val port = (server.localAddress() as InetSocketAddress).port Socket(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), port).use { a -> Socket(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), port).use { b -> val aIn = a.getInputStream().bufferedReader(UTF_8) val bIn = b.getInputStream().bufferedReader(UTF_8) a.getOutputStream().write("SLOW\n".toByteArray(UTF_8)) Thread.sleep(50) val t0 = System.nanoTime() b.getOutputStream().write("FAST\n".toByteArray(UTF_8)) // lag probe: how long until a trivial task runs on the loop? val lagMs = group.next().submit(Callable { (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 }).get(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS) val fast = bIn.readLine() val fastMs = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 println(if (dispatch) "[dispatch to app pool]" else "[blocking in the handler]") println(" event-loop lag probe: $lagMs ms") println(" FAST reply after $fastMs ms: $fast") println(" SLOW reply: ${aIn.readLine()}") } } server.close().sync() } finally { group.shutdownGracefully(0, 1, TimeUnit.SECONDS).sync() // close channels and loops first... blockingPool.shutdown() // ...then the pool they write from } }

try.expect: Blocking: both the probe and the FAST reply wait about a second (1,010 and 1,011 ms here), and every reply comes from the event-loop thread. Dispatch: the probe reads 0 to a few ms, FAST answers in a few ms, and both replies come from app-blocking-pool. The work is the same; only the thread that waits changed.

sections.html:
In Netty 4.2, ByteBufAllocator.DEFAULT is no longer the pooled allocator most 4.1 code and blog posts assume: it is an AdaptiveByteBufAllocator, and a plain buffer(16) comes back as a direct AdaptiveByteBuf. The migration guide says most workloads should see less memory use and that it was designed to work well with virtual threads. -Dio.netty.allocator.type=pooled brings back the old pooled allocator if you need it.

io_uring graduated from the incubator to a first-class transport. The package is now io.netty.channel.uring, the classes start with IoUring, and you use it like the others: MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup with IoUringIoHandler.newFactory() and the IoUring channel classes. Lesson 8 measures it against epoll.

TLS clients now verify the server's hostname by default. Code that relied on the old behavior to connect to a test server with a mismatched certificate will start failing its handshake.

netty-codec was split into smaller modules, and the minimum Java version is now 8. And Netty 4.1 and 4.2 cannot be on the same classpath. That one matters in practice: Vert.x 5.2.3 pins Netty 4.2.20.Final, so a library that drags Netty 4.1 jars in next to it fails at runtime in confusing ways instead of with a clear version conflict. Check ./gradlew dependencies for mixed io.netty versions before you debug anything else.

The threading rules did not change. A channel still belongs to one loop, handlers still run on it, and blocking it is still the most common way to make a Netty service slow.

try.title: Switch the transport
steps: In EventLoopDemo, change both groups to EpollIoHandler.newFactory() and the channel class to EpollServerSocketChannel.class (on macOS use KQueueIoHandler and KQueueServerSocketChannel). Run it. Predict first: do the thread names or the round-robin change?
Now put the channel class back to NioServerSocketChannel.class but keep the epoll (or kqueue) factory. Predict what happens before you run it.
try.expect: With matching factory and channel class the output looks the same: same thread names, same round-robin, because the threading model doesn't depend on the transport. With a mismatch the bind fails at once with IllegalStateException: incompatible event loop type: io.netty.channel.SingleThreadIoEventLoop: an NIO channel can only register with a loop whose IO handler is NIO. That is why the 4.2 migration guide reminds you to configure the channel class as well as the factory.

analogy: A channel pipeline is the mail line in an office. Letters come in at the door, one clerk opens the envelopes (the frame decoder), the next reads the handwriting (the string decoder), and the last one writes the answer. Replies go back down the same line the other way, and a typist (the encoder) turns them into print before they leave. The event loop is one worker who carries each letter through every station for a fixed set of mailboxes. The analogy breaks because real clerks work at the same time. In Netty one thread carries each message through every handler, which is exactly why one slow station stops the whole line.
world: Every HTTP request to your Quarkus services arrives through a Netty pipeline: Vert.x runs its HTTP server on Netty event loops, so a blocked Vert.x event loop is a blocked Netty event loop. The same holds for other clients you probably run: Lettuce for Redis and the AWS SDK's async HTTP client are built on Netty too. When a payment API's p99 jumps while CPU is low, a thread dump that shows an event-loop thread inside JDBC, Thread.sleep or a synchronized block is the first thing to look for. When you upgrade Quarkus, also check that nothing in the build still pulls in Netty 4.1.
mistake: The common mistake is calling something blocking from a handler because "it's only a few milliseconds": a JDBC lookup, a CompletableFuture.get(), a synchronous HTTP client, even logging to a slow appender. A few milliseconds per message on a loop that serves 2,000 connections is a queue that never drains under load. The 4.1-era fix, addLast(eventExecutorGroup, handler), is deprecated in 4.2. Dispatch the blocking part to your own executor and call ctx.writeAndFlush with the result, or move the work to a non-blocking client.

compare.title: Offloading a slow lookup from a Netty handler

java.title: QuoteHandler.java
java.html: final class QuoteHandler extends SimpleChannelInboundHandler<String> { private final Executor blocking; private final Function<String, String> lookup; QuoteHandler(Executor blocking, Function<String, String> lookup) { this.blocking = blocking; this.lookup = lookup; } @Override protected void channelRead0(ChannelHandlerContext ctx, String line) { blocking.execute(() -> ctx.writeAndFlush(lookup.apply(line) + "\n")); } }

kotlin.title: QuoteHandler.kt
kotlin.html: class QuoteHandler( private val blocking: Executor, private val lookup: (String) -> String, ) : SimpleChannelInboundHandler<String>() { override fun channelRead0(ctx: ChannelHandlerContext, line: String) { blocking.execute { ctx.writeAndFlush(lookup(line) + "\n") } } }

compare.note: At runtime these are the same class: Netty sees a SimpleChannelInboundHandler<String>, and the Kotlin lambda becomes a Runnable through SAM conversion. Kotlin saves the constructor boilerplate and takes a function type where Java needs Function<String, String>. One Kotlin-only temptation is worth naming: calling runBlocking { } inside channelRead0 to use a suspend function. That blocks the event loop just like Thread.sleep. If you want coroutines, launch on a scope with its own dispatcher and call ctx.writeAndFlush from the coroutine, which is the same manual dispatch with a different executor.

worked.title: Offload a handler without racing on its state

steps.say: A handler counts the authorizations it has served on each connection and calls a card issuer that takes 120 ms. It blocks the loop. The field served is safe only because one thread touches it.
steps.code: final class AuthHandler extends SimpleChannelInboundHandler<AuthRequest> { private int served; // per-connection state @Override protected void channelRead0(ChannelHandlerContext ctx, AuthRequest req) { AuthResponse res = issuer.authorize(req); // 120 ms, on the event loop served++; ctx.writeAndFlush(res.withSequence(served)); } }

alt.html: class AuthHandler : SimpleChannelInboundHandler<AuthRequest>() { private var served = 0 // per-connection state override fun channelRead0(ctx: ChannelHandlerContext, req: AuthRequest) { val res = issuer.authorize(req) // 120 ms, on the event loop served++ ctx.writeAndFlush(res.withSequence(served)) } }

steps.say: Moving everything into the executor frees the loop but breaks the counter. Two requests on the same connection now run on two pool threads at once, and served++ is a read-modify-write race on a plain field.
steps.code: blockingPool.execute(() -> { AuthResponse res = issuer.authorize(req); served++; // two pool threads, one field: lost updates ctx.writeAndFlush(res.withSequence(served)); });

alt.html: blockingPool.execute { val res = issuer.authorize(req) served++ // two pool threads, one field: lost updates ctx.writeAndFlush(res.withSequence(served)) }

steps.say: Do only the blocking call in the pool, then hop back to the channel's loop for everything that touches handler state. The loop is the lock.
steps.code: @Override protected void channelRead0(ChannelHandlerContext ctx, AuthRequest req) { blockingPool.execute(() -> { AuthResponse res = issuer.authorize(req); // 1. block off the loop ctx.executor().execute(() -> { // 2. back on the channel's loop served++; // 3. confined state, no lock needed ctx.writeAndFlush(res.withSequence(served)); }); }); }

alt.html: override fun channelRead0(ctx: ChannelHandlerContext, req: AuthRequest) { blockingPool.execute { val res = issuer.authorize(req) // 1. block off the loop ctx.executor().execute { // 2. back on the channel's loop served++ // 3. confined state, no lock needed ctx.writeAndFlush(res.withSequence(served)) } } }

steps.say: One thing the loop no longer gives you is order. Two requests on one connection can finish in either order, so replies can overtake each other. Either carry a correlation id the client matches on (most payment protocols do), or keep one request in flight per connection by turning off auto-read until the reply is written. Lesson 4 shows AUTO_READ.

lab.title: Build a quote server on Netty 4.2 and keep its loop free
steps: Run the tests. All four fail with NotImplementedError.

Write QuotePipeline.handlers: LineBasedFrameDecoder(MAX_LINE), StringDecoder(UTF_8), StringEncoder(UTF_8), then business. Write UpperCaseHandler.channelRead0. The two EmbeddedChannel tests should now pass.

Build QuoteServer as its KDoc describes: one-thread MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup with NioIoHandler.newFactory(), a ServerBootstrap with NioServerSocketChannel, and a ChannelInitializer that adds QuotePipeline.handlers(QuoteHandler(blocking, lookup)). Run the tests: three pass, and the slow-lookup test reports an event-loop lag near a second.
Fix QuoteHandler: run the lookup on blocking and call ctx.writeAndFlush from there. Run the tests until all four pass.
hints: ch.pipeline().addLast(*QuotePipeline.handlers(...)) uses Kotlin's spread operator to pass the array as varargs.
Create a new QuoteHandler inside initChannel. A handler without @Sharable may only sit in one pipeline, and the server has many channels.
bind(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), 0) picks a free port; port() reads it back from the channel.
The test's lag probe is server.group.next().submit(Callable { ... }). With one loop in the group, next() is always that loop.

drill.title: Write a Netty 4.2 bootstrap from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Write the code that starts a Netty 4.2 echo server on port 9000 with one acceptor loop, the default number of worker loops, and a handler that echoes each message back. Which class replaces NioEventLoopGroup, and why doesn't the echo handler release the message?

answer.html: EventLoopGroup boss = new MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup(1, NioIoHandler.newFactory()); EventLoopGroup workers = new MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup(NioIoHandler.newFactory()); Channel server = new ServerBootstrap() .group(boss, workers) .channel(NioServerSocketChannel.class) .childHandler(new ChannelInitializer<SocketChannel>() { @Override protected void initChannel(SocketChannel ch) { ch.pipeline().addLast(new ChannelInboundHandlerAdapter() { @Override public void channelRead(ChannelHandlerContext ctx, Object msg) { ctx.writeAndFlush(msg); // the write takes ownership and releases it once sent } }); } }) .bind(9000).sync().channel(); // MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup + NioIoHandler.newFactory() replaces NioEventLoopGroup.

alt.html: val boss = MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup(1, NioIoHandler.newFactory()) val workers = MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup(NioIoHandler.newFactory()) val server = ServerBootstrap() .group(boss, workers) .channel(NioServerSocketChannel::class.java) .childHandler(object : ChannelInitializer<SocketChannel>() { override fun initChannel(ch: SocketChannel) { ch.pipeline().addLast(object : ChannelInboundHandlerAdapter() { override fun channelRead(ctx: ChannelHandlerContext, msg: Any) { ctx.writeAndFlush(msg) // the write takes ownership and releases it once sent } }) } }) .bind(9000).sync().channel() // MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup + NioIoHandler.newFactory() replaces NioEventLoopGroup.

recap: An EventLoop is one thread with a selector and a task queue. A channel is registered with one loop for life, so its handlers never run concurrently.
Netty 4.2 builds groups as new MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup(n, NioIoHandler.newFactory()); NioEventLoopGroup and its cousins are deprecated. The default size is 2 × cores.
Inbound events flow from head to tail through decoders to your handler. Writes flow toward the head through encoders, starting at the current handler when you use ctx.
EmbeddedChannel runs a pipeline without a socket: writeInbound, readOutbound and finish() make handlers easy to test.
Never block a handler. Dispatch the slow part to your own executor and call ctx.writeAndFlush from there; the per-handler EventExecutorGroup overloads are deprecated in 4.2.

explain.prompt: Explain why a Netty handler that runs a 200 ms JDBC query slows down clients that never send that query, and how you would fix it in Netty 4.2.
explain.answer: Each channel is registered with one event loop for its whole life, and a loop is a single thread that runs the handlers of all its channels one event at a time. While the handler waits 200 ms for JDBC, that thread can't read, decode or write for any other channel on the same loop, so their requests queue behind the query. The fix in 4.2 is manual dispatch: in the handler, hand the query to an application executor sized for blocking work (or virtual threads), and call ctx.writeAndFlush with the result from that executor. Netty queues the write back onto the channel's loop. If the code needs handler state, hop back with ctx.executor().execute first. The deprecated addLast(EventExecutorGroup, ...) is not the answer anymore.

deeper.html:
Two details make manual dispatch work, and both are worth reading in Netty's source.

First, every outbound call checks where it runs. AbstractChannelHandlerContext.write asks executor.inEventLoop(). On the loop, it calls the next handler directly. Off the loop, it wraps the write in a task and puts it on the loop's queue. That is why ctx.writeAndFlush from your pool is safe, and also why it is not free: each one is a task hand-off and a wake-up of the selector.

Second, the loop interleaves IO and tasks. A Netty 4.2 loop is a SingleThreadIoEventLoop: it runs the IO handler (select and process ready channels), then drains its task queue, then selects again. Tasks you submit from other threads, writes from your pool, and timers all share the thread with IO. The 4.2 migration guide mentions hooks to measure how long IO processing and task processing take per loop run, for exactly this kind of tuning.

When you dispatch, think about the order of replies on a connection, as the worked example showed, and about backpressure: if the pool is slower than the arrival rate, its queue grows without bound unless something stops reading. Lesson 4 covers AUTO_READ and writability, which are Netty's tools for that.

To catch accidental blocking in tests, Netty ships an integration for BlockHound (Hidden$NettyBlockHoundIntegration in netty-common). BlockHound itself is a separate Java agent library. Installed in a test, it throws when code on a Netty event-loop thread calls a known blocking method such as Thread.sleep or a socket read.
